claims.text: The starting alloy is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a homogeneous, disordered, single-phase solid solution.
Approximately 3 at.% Nb is to be substituted for Ti in the starting alloy.
Minor Nb substitution in CoCrFeNiTi will induce nanoscale chemical ordering or nano-precipitate formation.
Ordered regions or fine precipitates can strengthen high-entropy alloys.
The proposed nanoscale ordered regions or precipitates impede dislocation motion.
Nb specifically promotes local chemical ordering or fine precipitate formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Minor compositional changes in other high-entropy alloys can produce strengthening associated with ordered phases or precipitated particles.
The Nb-modified alloy will have greater hardness than baseline CoCrFeNiTi.
The Nb-modified alloy will have greater compressive yield strength than baseline CoCrFeNiTi.
The Nb-modified alloy will retain good compressive plasticity relative to the baseline alloy.
The predicted combination of increased strength and retained plasticity will occur at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
Ta and W additions in a different VCrFeTaW alloy system increased compressive strength while decreasing plastic strain.
An ordered B2 matrix and solid-solution strengthening were associated with high ambient- and elevated-temperature strength in AlNbTiVZr0.25.
The hypothesis is limited to compressive loading from 25 °C to 600 °C at constant strain rate and comparable processing history.

contradictions.description: The phrase 'approximately 3 at.% Nb for Ti' implies about 3 at.% Nb in the complete alloy, whereas CoCrFeNiTi0.97Nb0.03 normalizes to only about 0.6 at.% Nb because the full formula contains five total atomic-ratio units.

The prediction emphasizes strengthening without sacrificing plasticity, but the cited Ta/W study reports that increasing strengthening additions decreased plastic strain and that further Laves-phase growth sharply deteriorated compressive performance. This does not directly refute the proposed Nb alloy, but it conflicts with the asserted general trend of strength retention without a ductility penalty.
